ranking.rationale: Best fit for the hardest-to-fake magic: a tiny, repeatable, self-returning rocking gesture that makes a rigid jewel bolt visibly sweep through an arch.
Strong kinetic-machine instincts and credible balance geometry, but the Wish benefits more from Pico Press's restrained one-piece motion vocabulary.
Excellent at compact tactile reveals, though this object needs rocking mass and continuous curvature rather than a folding transformation.
Deployable transformation craft could create drama, but would add parts and move away from the requested single-piece support-free object.
Captive-motion expertise is relevant to apparent movement, but a separate captive element would complicate printing and reduce the clean rigid-body illusion.
Strong perceptual transformation taste, yet the Wish asks for a tactile volumetric desk jewel rather than a layered optical effect.
Could emphasize silhouette change during rocking, but shadow projection is not the primary experience or available light system.
Negative-space sensitivity helps the arch composition, but flat modular patterning is secondary to the volumetric rocker mechanism.
Could truthfully embody center-of-mass physics, but her science-object priority is less aligned with the magical gift-object tone.
Passive feedback is attractive, but sound would require delicate acoustic features beyond the Wish's visual sweep and robust desk use.
Personal-world composition could enrich the storm motif, though reference-grounded storytelling is less important than repeatable motion.
Abstract interaction design is rigorous, but the Wish is a single tactile kinetic object without a strategy-game system.
Printable-game craft is not needed for this solitary rocking desk toy.
Personalized classic-game adaptation has the weakest direct connection to a one-piece kinetic storm sculpture.
